name: Colosseum
info: The Colosseum is the elliptical amphitheatre in the centre of Rome, begun under Vespasian in 72 and completed under Titus in 80, the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built and a lasting symbol of Imperial Rome.

facts.made: Built for the Flavian emperors: begun by Vespasian, finished by Titus and remodelled by Domitian; professional Roman builders, engineers and decorators, with slaves and prisoners of war often assumed to have formed much of the workforce
facts.form: A free-standing elliptical amphitheatre of travertine, tuff and Roman concrete, 189 metres long and 156 metres wide, with an outer wall 48 metres high, an arena 87 by 55 metres and the underground hypogeum beneath it
facts.where: In the centre of Rome, just east of the Roman Forum, between the Caelian, Esquiline and Palatine Hills
facts.known: gladiatorial contests and animal hunts; seating for an estimated 50,000 to 80,000; the velarium awning worked by sailors; the hypogeum of tunnels and lifts; medieval reuse as housing, fortress and quarry; the Good Friday Way of the Cross

t: Vespasian built the Colosseum on the site of Nero's artificial lake, funding it from the spoils of the First Jewish–Roman War, and placed it at the heart of the city rather than on its outskirts.
It hosted gladiatorial shows, animal hunts, executions and other spectacles for centuries; gladiatorial fights are last mentioned around 435 and animal hunts continued until at least 523.
Earthquakes and stone robbers ruined much of it, but from 1749 the popes treated it as a sacred site of the martyrs, protected it and began its long restoration.
dyk: Spectators were given tickets in the form of numbered pottery shards, and the passageways that let them reach and leave their seats in minutes were called vomitoria, from the Latin word for a rapid discharge.
ev: Construction of the amphitheatre began under the emperor Vespasian
Titus completed the top level, and the inaugural games were held in 80 or 81
A major fire, caused by lightning according to Dio Cassius, destroyed the wooden upper levels of the interior
Gladiatorial fights are last mentioned, after Honorius had banned them in 399 and again in 404
A great earthquake brought down the outer south side, and much of the fallen stone was reused across Rome
Pope Benedict XIV forbade quarrying, consecrated the building to the Passion of Christ and installed Stations of the Cross
The arena substructure was fully exposed under Benito Mussolini
A major restoration programme began, running until 2000

sections.origins:
The Colosseum stands on the floor of a low valley between the Caelian, Esquiline and Palatine Hills, through which a canalised stream ran. By the 2nd century BCE the area was densely inhabited. After the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE, Nero seized much of it for his own domain and built the Domus Aurea there, with an artificial lake surrounded by pavilions, gardens and porticoes, and the gigantic bronze Colossus of Nero at its entrance.

Under Vespasian much of the Domus Aurea was torn down, the lake was filled in and the land reused for the new amphitheatre. Building on Nero's lake can be seen as a populist gesture, returning to the people a part of the city that Nero had appropriated. Unlike many amphitheatres, which stood on the outskirts of a city, the Colosseum was placed in the city centre, symbolically and geographically at the heart of Rome. Its construction was funded by the spoils taken from the Jewish Temple after the First Jewish–Roman War; a reconstructed inscription found on the site records that "the emperor Vespasian ordered this new amphitheatre to be erected from his general's share of the booty."
sections.content:
The Colosseum is an entirely free-standing structure whose architecture derives from two theatres placed back to back. Elliptical in plan, it is 189 metres long and 156 metres wide, and its outer wall rises 48 metres. The surviving façade has three superposed storeys of arcades framed by engaged columns of the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders, topped by an attic with Corinthian pilasters. Two hundred and forty mast corbels supported the velarium, a retractable awning of canvas and ropes worked by sailors from the naval headquarters at Misenum.

Eighty entrances ringed the building, 76 of them for ordinary spectators; the northern main entrance was reserved for the emperor. Seating reflected the stratified order of Roman society: boxes for the emperor and the Vestal Virgins, a podium for senators, tiers for the equites and for richer and poorer citizens, and at the top a gallery for the common poor, slaves and women. Beneath the sand-covered wooden floor of the arena lay the hypogeum, a two-level network of tunnels and cages with eighty vertical shafts, lifts and pulleys that raised animals and scenery to the surface.
sections.making:
Construction began under Vespasian in around 70–72 CE (73–75 according to some sources). The building had reached the third storey by Vespasian's death in 79; his son Titus finished the top level in 80, and the inaugural games were held in 80 or 81. Vespasian's younger son Domitian remodelled it further, building the hypogeum and adding a gallery at the top to increase its capacity.

It is often assumed, as with many Roman projects of the time, that slaves and prisoners of war contributed much of the unskilled labour, while teams of professional builders, engineers, artists, painters and decorators carried out the specialised work. The materials included wood, limestone, tuff, tiles, cement and mortar, with Roman concrete for foundations, corridor vaults and secondary walls. The outer wall is estimated to have required over 100,000 cubic metres of travertine, set without mortar and held together by 300 tons of iron clamps. The hypogeum was restructured many times: at least twelve phases of construction can be seen.
sections.reception:
The shows held in the Colosseum, called munera, were always given by private individuals rather than the state; they had a strong religious element but were also demonstrations of power and family prestige, and were immensely popular. Animal hunts used beasts imported mainly from Africa and the Middle East. Trajan is said to have celebrated his Dacian victories in 107 with contests involving 11,000 animals and 10,000 gladiators over 123 days. Condemned people were executed by beasts during the lunch intervals, and ancient writers recorded mock sea battles in the early years, though historians debate how the arena could have been flooded.

Honorius banned gladiator fights in 399 and again in 404, and they are last mentioned around 435; animal hunts continued until at least 523. Christians generally regard the Colosseum as a site where many believers were martyred. Other scholars hold that most martyrdoms took place elsewhere in Rome, notably the Circus Maximus. In the Middle Ages the building was not on pilgrims' itineraries, but in 1653 Fioravante Martinelli listed it first among places sacred to the martyrs, and in 1749 Pope Benedict XIV declared it sanctified by their blood, a claim for which there is no historical evidence.
sections.survival:
A fire in 217 destroyed the wooden upper levels, and repairs followed until about 240, in 250 or 252 and in 320; an inscription records restoration under Theodosius II and Valentinian III, possibly after an earthquake in 443. After the games ended, a chapel was built into the structure, the arena became a cemetery and the vaulted spaces were rented out as housing and workshops. Around 1200 the Frangipani family fortified it as a castle. The earthquake of 1349 brought down the outer south side, and the fallen stone was reused for palaces, churches and hospitals. The marble façade was burned for quicklime, and the iron clamps were hacked out, leaving pockmarks that still scar the walls.

A religious confraternity restored part of it in 1377 and lived in its northern section until the early 19th century. Benedict XIV's ban on quarrying in 1749 marked a turn; later popes cleared vegetation, reinforced the façade with brick wedges in 1807 and 1827 and repaired the interior. The substructure was partly excavated in 1810–1814 and 1874 and fully exposed in the 1930s. A restoration of 1993–2000 was followed by a privately sponsored cleaning and repair of the façade, completed in 2016.
sections.legacy:
The Colosseum remains a renowned symbol of Imperial Rome and one of the city's most visited sites, listed among the New 7 Wonders of the World and shown on the Italian 5 euro cent coin. The name itself, believed to come from the nearby Colossus of Nero, passed into medieval and modern languages; by the early 16th century the French colisée could mean any amphitheatre. An 8th-century epigram attributed to the Venerable Bede, "as long as the Colossus stands, so shall Rome", is often misread as referring to the building.

Its Christian associations continue: each Good Friday the pope leads a torchlit Way of the Cross procession to the amphitheatre, and crosses stand around the arena. Since 2000 the city has lit the building in gold whenever a death sentence somewhere is commuted or a jurisdiction abolishes capital punishment. Architects have copied or echoed it, from the unfinished Nazi Kongresshalle in Nuremberg and Mussolini's Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana to the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum and the Vancouver Public Library, and it appeared on Olympic medals from 1928 to 2000.

summary: The Colosseum, begun by Vespasian in 72 and finished by Titus in 80, was Rome's great amphitheatre for gladiatorial shows and animal hunts until the 6th century. Fire, earthquakes and stone robbers ruined much of it, and it served as housing, fortress and quarry before the popes made it a shrine of the martyrs and began its restoration.
